utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Davis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher. I would like the witness to be shown what has previously been admitted as P380.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the guidelines for the criteria for criminal prosecution which were made in 1992 by the military prosecutor's office at the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army. And these guideline contain instructions indicating how to proceed that laws on criminal procedure and criminal codes should be complied with and that perpetrators of criminal offenses should be prosecuted in accordance with these laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this document in force and effect throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was in effect in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could have you turn in your version to the page that's marked 00760352. And in the English version it would be 008114 -- 4383, excuse me. I would like to direct your attention to the underlined heading that's marked number 3, which appears to begin a section addressing guidelines for -- sorry. I'll let you get to the page.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's 00760352.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please just tell me what the page is. Perhaps it would be easier that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 11 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I would like to direct your attention to the underlined heading that's marked number 3, towards the bottom of the page. And it appears to begin a section addressing guidelines for criminal offenses against humanity and international law, pursuant to chapter 16 of the criminal code. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the B/C/S version there are some blank pages, so you'll have to turn two pages over. If you could read the paragraph that begins at the bottom of that page under heading number 3 and then continuing to page 12. I would like to just give you a moment to look that over.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean to start right from the beginning, the legal classification of criminal offenses from this chapter has been adopted from international conventions with some adaptation and closer definition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want you to read it out loud. I just wanted you to read it to yourself and take a moment to review it.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I know you've had an opportunity to see this document when you met with me in my office yesterday. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 12 in your version, which is 00760354, the third paragraph down the page refers to some criminal offenses, specific criminal offenses under the criminal code. Do you see those references?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it indicates that the criminal law applied in the territory of the Republika Srpska defines 16 criminal offenses against humanity and international law, including genocide, war crimes against the civilian population, war crimes against the wounded and the sick and against prisoners of war. Are you familiar with the legal references that are mentioned here in this document?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you agree with this document, that those laws referred to there were in effect in the Republika Srpska in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn to the page 14 in your version, which is 00760358. In the English version, for those who are using that copy, it's 00814384. The second and third paragraph on that page -- the first full paragraph and the paragraph following that appear to address obligations of the VRS with respect to violations of the laws that are outlined and described previously in the document. Can you tell the Court what this document indicates about the duties of officers of the VRS with respect to preventing and reporting violations of crimes against humanity and international law.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states that if somebody has learned to -- that a criminal offence has been committed, that they are duty-bound to take certain action and to submit criminal reports with the -- to the competent military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need to look at that document anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: You can -- if I would ask the usher to please provide the witness with the document that has been previously marked as P715 for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll ask you also with respect to this document whether it's something that you recognise.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the criminal code of the former socialist federative republic of Yugoslavia, which was also in force in the Republika Srpska, because until 1992 we did not have our own laws. And then a decision was passed that the criminal code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was styled, be in force. This is the general part of the criminal code, and we also had the special part of the law, which was the law of the socialist republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So this criminal code, was it in force and effect throughout the war in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was in effect in the Republika Srpska in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like for you to turn to the page marked 00253459 in the B/C/S version. This would be the first page of the English version. And the page number of the book is 67, if that helps. This page indicates at the top, chapter 16, criminal offenses against humanity and international law. Then it goes on to list various offenses, the first one being Article 141, genocide. Do you see what I'm referring to there?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are these the laws to which the guidelines that we were just looking through were referring?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The guidelines referred to the entire criminal procedure, criminal prosecution, and that would mean that this was also included in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all we need from that document. I'd like to ask you a few questions now, having briefly discussed the legal basis for criminal prosecutions during the war. I'd like to ask you a few questions about how the criminal code was enforced as a practical matter. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how investigations or subsequent prosecutions were initiated in the military court system during the war.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The competent organ submitted the criminal report to the military prosecutor's office. The military prosecutor's office in turn, when it received the criminal report, had several options. If there wasn't sufficient evidence, they could reject the criminal report. If there was something missing, they could order that additional information be gathered. If the criminal -- if the prosecutor's office deemed that there were grounds for the suspicion, then they could submit the request for the investigation to be conducted, which was conducted by an by an investigative judge of the military court. After the investigation was completed, the entire file was submitted to the prosecutor and the prosecutor again had several options. If the prosecutor deemed that there was sufficient evidence and material for an indictment to be filed, he could do that. If there wasn't enough evidence of the criminal offence, he could order that the investigation be stopped. Or if he deemed that there could be some additional information gathered, he could order the investigation to be re-opened and for additional information to be gathered. That was the procedure. The moment the report was filed with the prosecutor's office, it was given a special number in the logbook. And it had the same reference number throughout the procedure. And then for trial, the trial was conducted before the military court. That would, in brief, be the procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned after a competent organ submitted a report concerning a potential crime. Who could submit such reports?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such reports, since we were dealing with military personnel mostly, they would be filed by unit commanders, security personnel, military police, in fact any military person or any civilian, in fact, if they had information that a criminal offence had been committed could file such a report. And the military prosecutor was bound to act on it. Now, whether he would eventually file the indictment or not, that was up to him. But he had to act on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say that the military prosecutor was bound to act on it in some way, and you've described several different ways that they would proceed from that point after a report was filed. You also mentioned that when the report was filed, the case would be assigned a number in a logbook. Was every report that was filed entered into the logbook that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules, every criminal report had to be recorded in the logbook. If the military prosecutor failed to do so, that would constitute a breach of the procedure. And then records could be kept of the file at each stage of the procedure. You could follow it through various stages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So if a formal report was filed by a VRS officer against any VRS personnel, as required by the guidelines we've previously reviewed, whether the charge was one of collaboration with the enemy, desertion, whatever the charge, you would expect that charge to appear in the logbook that you've described. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If such a charge was made, that would be recorded. And after the prosecutor filed such charges, then again we would have a record of a trial, if any, and judgement, if any. Again, as I said, there would be records all the way through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you -- yesterday when we were speaking about your employment history, you mentioned that the military courts were dissolved in May of 2000. Do you know what happened to records from the military courts at that time?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the instructions we received from the Ministry of Defence, all files were transferred to the jurisdiction of certain districts in accordance with the location of the actual perpetration of crime. Pending files were handed over and all the files that have already been adjudicated on were also handed over. So our archives were also handed over. The files of the military Supreme Court were handed over to the Supreme Court. And all the cases before the basic court and basic military prosecutor's office were transferred to civilian courts and prosecutor's office, according to the territorial jurisdiction. So it was either to the district or basic courts and prosecutor's office, depending on the actual gravity of the crime; that was also a criterion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where records of crimes that were committed in and around Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik went after the dissolution of the military courts in May 2000?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the dissolution of military courts and prosecutor's office, all cases that dealt with war crimes were transferred to the district military -- district prosecutor's offices and courts, because they had subject matter jurisdiction over those crimes. If there were any cases regarding Srebrenica before military prosecutors' offices, they would have been transferred to the district prosecutor's office in Bijeljina or the district court in Bijeljina. But since things were done in accordance with the wrong [as interpreted] rules, they were handed over to the district -- they would have been handed over to the district prosecutor's office in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you: When you took over as district prosecutor in Bijeljina, in May 2001, were there any pending cases involving war crimes by the VRS against Muslim victims, following the fall of Srebrenica, that were transferred to your district?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no such cases, pending or otherwise before the district prosecutor's office or court in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And going -- returning to the position you held before that, when you became a military -- the military prosecutor in April 2000, were there any cases on the dockets of the basic military courts that you supervised at that stage involving war crimes by the VRS against Muslim victims following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally: During your time as a judge on the Supreme Court, were any cases, appellant cases, brought before that court that involved war crimes by VRS against Muslim victims following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher. I would like to show the witness -- the document has been marked as P713 for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this document in my office yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me whether you had seen the document at any time before I showed it to you in my office yesterday.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, an order was discussed. I don't know whether I had actually seen it or not, but I do know that it was a topic of discussion, an order of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether it was a topic of discussion in 1996, when it was apparently created, or whether it was discussed at some other time, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document appears to refer to a request by President Karadzic for an investigation into crimes after the fall of Srebrenica. Are you personally aware -- are you personally aware of any investigation of this nature that actually took place in 1996 or in the several years following?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of what had been done as regards those investigations. I know that this was a topic that was talked about, the investigations that would have to be carried out. But as to what had actually been done, I don't know about it, and this was not actually in the scope of my activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher one more time, I'd like to show the witness what has marked for identification as P714.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll give you just a moment to look that over. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it in your office, but not before that. This is the information from the Minister Kijac, who signed this letter, and it pertains to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this report or any related investigation?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If the usher could please show the witness a document that has been marked as P712 for identification purposes. If I could just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a document we've marked for identification as P712. I believe part of this document was tendered under seal by the Defence yesterday as 67/3. But as I recall, it was just a part of what here is a larger document. So we'll tender it in a different form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to please show the witness page 02146508 of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just give you a moment to look that over.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: The English ERN for the page that the witness is looking at is 03037619.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you ever seen this order before?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm seeing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it appear to you to be?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is an order given by Karadzic ordering that a commission be established in order to investigate the matters concerning two corpses that had been found, to have that investigated. And as far as I can see, a commission had been established, because it is mentioned here that there were two people present from the security centre, Vasic, Dragomir, from the Bijeljina centre; and then Marjanovic Radco from the MUP. I assume it was from Bijeljina, too. So therefore, they had been ordered to investigate this, and it says here that it was to be done in Zvornik security centre. They were to investigate this and to compile a written report and inform the president of the republic about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell from the face of this document whether this is related to crimes that followed the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say now. Obviously they didn't know even then where these two corpses had come from. They were not identified. And then it says here: On the battlefields of previous battles with the Muslim side, I don't know whether this was before the fall of Srebrenica or afterwards, the battlefield in Pilica was mentioned in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you personally have any information or knowledge of any investigation that followed from this order?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is this document from 1996. This was carried out by the security centre, so I was not in a position to know about this. I was a judge at the time and I had my cases. I don't know whether they informed the then-prosecutors about this, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like for you to look at another page of the document now which is -- the B/C/S version is 02146504. And it in English it would be 03037616 -- oh, I'm sorry, did I give the wrong page number? Are you looking at a blank page.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a blank page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 6505. Does that help? With respect to this document, Mr. Kovacevic, have you had a chance to look it over?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document. This was compiled by the military prosecutor, Predrag Drinic, and he states, himself, here, that he doesn't know what persons were involved, that this needs to be investigated, that he has been informed, and then it needs to be determined whether this falls under the jurisdiction of civilian courts, a civilian prosecutor or the military one, and that it needs to be determined how these -- how this has arrived here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My only question to you with respect to this document is whether you personally had any knowledge of -- or have any knowledge of whether such a commission was formed and whether an investigation took place.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: That's all I need with those documents, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the documents that you I've had a chance to review just now, did you personally ever become aware during your time working in the military court system during the war of any investigations or prosecutions of war crimes by the VRS against Muslims, following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any charges being filed by VRS commanders or officers against VRS personnel for war crimes against Muslim victims, following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such criminal reports in the office of the military prosecutor, at least I didn't see any when I came there. And there were no such reports filed after the dissolution of the military prosecutor's office. There were no such files filed in Bijeljina. They were not filed by anyone, by no commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've talked about the fact that you're now the chief prosecutor in the Bijeljina district. Is it true that you were visited by representatives of the ICTY in 2001 and asked to locate the logs that you've described and related paperwork in which war crimes committed by VRS personnel in the Bijeljina district would have been recorded?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to find those logbooks?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review them?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find any entries in those logbooks indicating that a charge had been filed by a VRS officer, any VRS officer against other VRS personnel relating to war crimes against Muslims, following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you some additional records now and ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what you can about them. The first one is marked for identification as P702. Can you tell us what this document appears to be.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information on the criminal activities in July of 1995 in the basic military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. So all basic military prosecutor's offices had to report on a monthly basis to the military prosecutor of the army of Republika Srpska on criminal activity on reports that were filed, requests to launch an investigation, and indictments issued for that month so that the military prosecutor would be kept abreast of their work. And I'm not quite sure whether the prosecutor in turn sent that information to the Ministry of Justice, or to the Main Staff, or perhaps to both of those places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If I could ask you to turn to the page marked 02158324 in the B/C/S version, it should be the second page. In the English version it's also the second page, which is 7477. In your version, Mr. Kovacevic, the last page -- the last paragraph at the bottom of the page, if you could read that over. And for those reading the English version, it's the paragraph before the heading that's II.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say page 2 or page 1?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The page marked 8324. It should be the second page of the document that you've holding, and the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's page 1 in my version, 8324.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read that last paragraph on the page?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here as it -- crime trends in July of 1995, bearing in mind a numerical situation according to the above figures -- no, I'm sorry. So bearing in mind the figures, we can see that there was a rise in the number of criminal reports filed. And since some reports have been referred to the Drina Corps in view of the expansion of the territorial jurisdiction of the military court in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we had some discussion about which military court district had jurisdiction over Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, and the surrounding areas in July 1995. Does this help to refresh your recollection as to which military court district had that jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the days' [as interpreted] accord and basic military -- basic prosecutor's office in Serbian Sarajevo had already been dissolved and transferred to these authorities. This is the conclusion that I can draw based on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that -- so who then, in your view, based on what you're seeing here had jurisdiction -- which military court district had jurisdiction over Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, and the surrounding areas in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can ask you to turn to page 8326 in the B/C/S version, and it's 7478 in the English version. If I can direct your attention to the heading marked number 3 that indicates crimes under chapter 16 of the KZ RS. Now, we looked at the criminal code earlier, and I believe you told us that this chapter 16 is crimes against humanity and international law. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does this report for July 1995 tell us regarding whether any charges or investigations, prosecutions, were initiated for war crimes in the Bijeljina district in that month?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It says here that there were no requests to launch an investigation and no indictments were issued for these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to show the witness is marked for identification as P703.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, if I can just ask you to tell us what this document appears to be.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, information for the month of August, compiled by the military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can turn in your version to the page in your version marked 02158558. And again, look at the heading marked number 3 for crimes under chapter 16 of the criminal code. What does this report tell us regarding whether any charges, investigations, or prosecutions were initiated for war crimes in the Bijeljina district in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that as far as these crimes under chapter 16 are concerned, that there were 210 requests to launch investigation, all 210 against civilian persons. And then it lists the names of certain persons, regarding whom there was a request to launch an investigation, and there's also a description of crimes they might have committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you've noticed, the next few paragraphs discuss some specific charges and indictments. Can you take a moment to review those and tell us whether you can discern the ethnicity of the perpetrators of the crimes charged and discussed here.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on their first and last names, it would seem that they are Muslims, or rather, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in August 1995, there were 210 war crimes charged against -- all against civilians. What does that indicate about whether any such charges were filed against VRS personnel in that month?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here regarding whom these requests were filed and there's also a number of such requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any indication of whether any charges were filed against any soldiers, VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to show the witness has been marked as P704.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could look at page 0215 -- well, first, can you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the report on criminal activity for the month of September 1995 in the office of the military prosecutor -- basic military prosecutor in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could turn to page 02158599 in your version. In the English version it's 03067466. And once again, I'm going to ask you to do this with each one of a few more documents. If you can look at the heading marked number 3, crimes under chapter 16, and tell us what you can discern about whether any charges, reports, requests for investigations, prosecutions, were executed for war crimes in Bijeljina in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that there were seven requests to launch an investigation, all seven against civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here again --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that one indictment was issued. And then it states the name of the person mentioned in the indictment and the number of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you discern from the information provided about the one indictment what the ethnicity of the charged individual was?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a Muslim -- a Bosniak, at least based on the first and last name, that would be my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The next document is P706. And if you can take a look at this document, both the cover page and the inside pages, and tell me what this document appears to you to be.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is information for October of 1995, and this is the military prosecutor's office in Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the second page of the document, not the cover page, but the first true page of the document, can you tell me what district this document appears to be discussing.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 2 it says that it was sent by the basic military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. It has their date and their number and the signature of the prosecutor, and it seems that the cover page was a mistake, because this seems to come from the office in Bijeljina. It must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the substance of the report that's attached to the cover page covers the district of Bijeljina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could turn to in your version page 02158571. And in the English version, it's 03067949. Once again, if you could look at the heading entitled number 3 and tell us what the report indicates regarding charges of war crimes in that month.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that in October there were no requests to launch an investigation and no indictments were issued concerning these crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document is P707. To save some time, I'll ask you if you agree with me that this seems to be a report for November 1995 from the Bijeljina district.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And turning to page 02157793 in your version and 03067936 in the English version. Would you agree with me that this indicates that there were no requests for investigation or prosecutions initiated in November 1995 in the Bijeljina district?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document is P708. Would you agree with me that this is a report for December 1995, crime trends in the Bijeljina district?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And turning to page 02157838 in your version and 03067924 in the English version under heading number 3, would you agree that there appear to be no requests for investigation or indictments, prosecutions, in that month for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document is P710. Would you agree with me that this is a similar report for January 1996?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at page 02158036 in your version, can you discern whether any charges, investigations, or prosecutions were initiated for war crimes in that month?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- I mean, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last document I'll have you look at is marked for identification as P711. And this is a February 1996 monthly report for Bijeljina. And I'll direct your attention to 02157959 in your version. And can you tell us whether there were any charges, investigations, prosecutions for war crimes in that month.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that as regards these crimes are concerned, that a request for investigation was filed regarding one person, and also the statement of reasons for the charges are stated here -- it's stated here, and also the very crime itself, that is a crime against civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you identify -- can you discern from the information that's provided here what the ethnicity of the victims of this crime were?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since this is a member of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, that would probably be a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring now to the perpetrator or the victim?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the perpetrator or the victim? It says here that victims were of Serbian ethnicity. Yes, yes, that's correct. Let me check. Yes, victims were of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, given the criminal code that we reviewed earlier regarding war crimes and the guidelines that we also saw, does it surprise you that there are no indications in these records of any reports, investigations, or prosecutions of war crimes by VRS personnel against Muslims after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in order to be able to understand the essence of this, I have to say that as far as I was able to observe during the war, criminal reports and investigations and requests for investigations and in some cases even indictments were issued mostly for persons belonging to other ethnic groups, because we were at war. And I have this feeling that the same thing was going on on the other sides, that they did it in a similar way. And I guess that if the people that had fled Srebrenica, they were at the disposal of the organs of the federation probably in Tuzla and so on. I assume that they could -- they were able to get their statements and gather other kinds of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, are you going to start your cross-examination or we have an early break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I leave it to the Court's discretion, Your Honour. I can start or we can take an early break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll have a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope you can see me with that contraption that's in front of you. I want to pick up with the last question that was posed to you by the Prosecutor, because you indicated that it was your understanding that the others, that is, on the federation side, the Muslims and the Croats were doing the same thing with respect to following up on complaints to the military tribunals. Okay?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any investigations or prosecutions against Alija Izetbegovic for the war crimes that he had committed during the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally am not aware of them, with the exception of what I have learned from the media or read in the papers. I know that some materials have been submitted to this Tribunal, and among other persons, this material concerned also Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What about with Naser Oric for some of the atrocities that he was committing on or about from 1992 to 1995, were you aware of any investigations that were done by the military courts on the federation side against Mr. Naser Oric who, as I understand, was openly walking about in Tuzla up until the time he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Naser Oric is concerned, I don't know what the military or other courts in the federation did in this regard. However, I am familiar with this case, as regards the Bijeljina military court and prosecutor's office, because the crimes committed by Naser Oric and his unit were committed in Bijeljina, Srebrenica, and Bratunac. That was the territorial jurisdiction of Bijeljina, and that's why I am aware of that. I am familiar with the file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But that's on the Serb side, on the RS side. With respect to the federation side, since the question was posed by the Prosecution, are you aware of on the federation side whether the military courts there did any investigations regarding Naser Oric who was openly bragging about some of the atrocities, and we have documentation in the Western press where he's openly bragging about his atrocities?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the federation. I don't know whether they did anything or whether they didn't do anything as regards the Naser Oric case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to -- that concludes that portion of that segment of the cross-examination on the point that was brought out by the Prosecutor. So now what I would like to do is talk a little bit about the function of the military courts, as they existed back then. Could you please tell us how they were established, under whose jurisdiction were they and how they were financed.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time, the military courts were attached to the Main Staff. And then after that, they were attached to the Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska. Do you mean the funding for the operation of the prosecutor's offices and the courts? If that's what you mean, they came from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska; in other words, from the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that initially they were under the Main Staff or attached to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Attached to the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska. That was for a brief period of time. And after that, they were under the Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would have been a civilian organ once they came under the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not a civilian organ. They were military organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I want to get to. Were they controlled by the military, in essence?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were, since this was the Ministry of Defence. We were attached to the Main Staff only for a very brief period of time. My personal opinion is that in order for people not to be influenced anymore, to prevent the people from working under the pressure of the army or of the Main Staff, that was the reason why the prosecutor's office was reattached to the Ministry of Defence of the national defence, in order to minimise the influence of the Main Staff. That is my assumption because I am not a politician and this is more or less a political issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But even after they were put under the Ministry of Defence, during this wartime period, from 1992 to 1995, would it be fair to say that the military prosecutor came under a great deal of pressure and influence from the military, and in particular, the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the pressure that was exerted. I know that we as judges were not under any kind of pressure in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, of course if you don't get any sensitive cases to judge, you're not going to come under any pressure. Right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a wartime situation, all cases are sensitive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But a case, for instance, that might be lodged against Mladic or Beara or Popovic, the security organs. Would you not say that those are slightly more sensitive and the pressure might be slightly more than if you're investigating some Muslim civilian who is accused of having committed crimes against some Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such cases, but had there been such cases, probably a person would pay much more attention and be much more circumspect with dealing with such cases. But that's only my assumption because such cases did not exist; there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were -- do you know whether those who worked in the military courts, either as judges or prosecutors, held a rank, a military rank?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They all had a military rank, because according to the adopted law on the military courts that existed in the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, in order for a person to be a military judge or military prosecutor, automatically that person would be given a certain rank. That was an automatic procedure. For instance, a judge of a basic court, a military court, or a basic military prosecutor had to have at least the rank of a captain. These ranks were given as a formality only. I can explain to you why, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when the war broke out, most of the officers, military judges who were active-duty personnel, left the country and went to the former Yugoslavia, Serbia, and Montenegro, together with the rest of the army, which means that the active-duty servicemen with law degrees and with ranks who were military judges and prosecutors simply did not exist. And then judges of regular courts and regular prosecutors were taken in, and the military judicial system was created. And these people were given appropriate ranks and the functions of military judges and prosecutors in their respective territories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, everyone, all citizens, were more or less mobilised from the age of 16 to 60 during that period of time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In May there was the mobilisation; it was declared. And those who failed to respond to the call-up faced criminal sanctions, which were quite severe in a wartime situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it safe for me to assume that those who were serving as judges and prosecutors in these military tribunals, that was part of their active duty, the mobilisation duty?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say that because only one or two people remained who were active-duty servicemen who had been active-duty servicemen before the war and who remained to work in the military judicial system of Republika Srpska. The others were simply mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just to make sure I understand you, the prosecutor, for instance, did he also have to be on the front line and carry out duties as a soldier, or was he carrying out his duties, his military duties, as the prosecutor, the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He carried out his military obligations as a military prosecutor. They never went to the front lines, and that went both for military prosecutors and military judges. They worked exclusively in their offices or on crime scenes to carry out on-site investigations, if that was possible at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, given your explanations, with the understanding that the military courts are under the Department of Defence, does it not appear to you that perhaps the military prosecutor and the military courts were essentially part of the military and not part of the civilian government?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was part of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And might that, to some degree, explain the difficulties someone might have, an officer might have, in going to a military organ and then filing a complaint or a report against someone, such as General Mladic or someone such as Colonel Beara, who was the head of the security organ for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such problems and I don't know whether others had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't have those problems because you were a judge. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it we have the wrong person here in court today if I'm going to pose these sorts of questions?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it's up to you to judge that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I'm not really sure that's a question that the witness can respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think he just did. I'll rephrase, I'll rephrase --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think your question is posed to the Prosecutor rather than the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'll rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, if I wanted to make these sorts of inquiries, pose these questions that I'm posing to you, from your answer it would appear that I would need to have a military prosecutor from that period on the stand and not a judge who served in the military courts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure that this is a question that's appropriate to be directed to this witness. In addition, the questions that Mr. Karnavas is referring to are speculative towards any witness, regardless of whether they were a military prosecutor or a military judge at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Karnavas has already rephrased this question in a way that is acceptable to this Bench. Witness, you may answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that at any rate for this period, a military prosecutor could give you better answers than a judge, as regards the manner of operation of the prosecutor. Of course I can give you answers as regards the manner of operation of a judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the reason I posed that question in the manner and fashion in which I did was because of your answers with respect to how a case developed from report to judgement. And I understand from your testimony elicited from the Prosecutor there, you indicated that reports for investigation would go to a prosecutor and not to a judge. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, in listening to your very cogent and quite clear answer as how a case developed, this is classic Romano-Germanique process that was being applied at the military tribunal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The law on criminal procedure is the same for regular courts, for military courts, for military prosecutors, the same law applied to all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, in listening to your previous answers, one might be left with the impression that perhaps the military tribunal of which the military prosecution was a member of might not necessarily be totally independent. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you are right. I'm sure that there were no direct -- there was no direct pressure. And now whether anyone had any reserves in this respect or not, I would assume that it had to do more with the personality of that person than with anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And of course again, you can only speak from the judge's point of view, not from the prosecutor's point of view. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the prosecutor would be duty-bound to at least follow-up on a report, should one be made to him or to her? You need to answer so we make a record.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Now, you were asked a series of questions as to who could initiate a report with the military prosecutor. And you said just about anyone. It could be military; it could be civilian. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in preparation to come here and testify, as I understand it, the Office of the Prosecution came to Bijeljina more than on one occasion to speak with you and to speak with Judge Radomir Aleksic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Judge Aleksic is the president currently of the court -- of the district court in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they by any chance, the Office of the Prosecution, explain to you anything about their case with respect to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigators that came went through our logbooks looking for some cases, I can't remember now the cases in question, but mostly those dealing with Srebrenica. We talked mostly about that event. Some of the materials that we had from the military judiciary were photocopied, parts of the logbook, some of the materials, documents, that we have now been through. So at no point were the investigators from The Hague prevented from having access to these documents. They could at any point go through any documents they wished and make photocopies. And that is exactly what the president of the district court, Mr. Aleksic, did, although in the actual fact his court did not have any such cases left -- there are no such cases left there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you what has been marked for identification -- what has been marked as an exhibit and I believe has been already admitted as an exhibit as P687/A. And perhaps you can give us your opinion on this. Have you by any chance, sir, had an opportunity to look at this decision on the appointment of the civilian commissioner for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you could take a moment, sir, and look at it, and in particular I would like you to look at -- I mean, pay a little closer attention to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in looking at paragraph 4, could you give us an opinion as to whether the civilian commissioner, which would have been Mr. Deronjic at the time, whether he would have been responsible for the civilians from Srebrenica who had gathered in Potocari after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was responsible. And in fact, this decision imposes this responsibility on him to treat them as war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it also allows the civilian population to choose where they will live or where they will move to. So this poses an obligation on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could also look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I wonder if this is the right question to ask this witness, this particular witness, about this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this question could be put to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we are dealing with a jurist. We are dealing with someone who was on the military courts at the time. The question was elicited from the Prosecutor whether anyone, including civilians. There is an issue, I believe, as to who is responsible ultimately for these prisoners. I think it is an underlying issue in this case. At the very minimum, it's for impeaching Mr. Deronjic who said he had no responsibility and it wasn't his responsibility for the well-being of those people. And I also would like to point out that Mr. Deronjic had an obligation to file a report as well. Now, I think this is also relevant to the fact that the Prosecutor had stood up - not this one but in another case - has stood up and said that it is absolutely -- they don't have sufficient evidence for Mr. Deronjic with respect to Srebrenica. And I think that this is highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, concerning the obligation to file a report, there may be some relevance here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at paragraph number 5, sir, and just look at it and read it.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Decisions of the civilian commissioner shall be binding upon all civilian authority organs in the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that include units of MUP?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from reading this decision, would Mr. Deronjic be one of those individuals required to file a report with the military prosecutor, given his authority?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this decision, he was duty-bound to ensure the implementation of this decision. And should he fail to do so, he will be partially liable, or he will be among those liable. And it would be up to the prosecution to determine just how liable he would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And from this could you give us a legal opinion, based on your knowledge of the RS law as it applied back then, whether these prisoners, as stated under paragraph 4, were the ultimate responsibility of Mr. Deronjic, or were they the ultimate responsibility of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this witness has enough information with which to respond to this question. He's an appropriate person to pose this question to, but I would object on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, if I may be heard for a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Davis has had this gentleman in there -- on their list for several months. They obviously went through the laws with him. They picked and chose the various laws they wanted to use this gentleman for. He is a jurist. He is a judge. He was a prosecutor at one point, the chief military prosecutor, now he's back to being a civilian prosecutor. Obviously, he would have sufficient knowledge. Now, if he doesn't, the gentleman can simply say, I don't have enough knowledge or information at this point in time, in which case perhaps I could assist him with some documents. And then later on, and then, you know, at a later point he could tell us whether he's able to give us a reasoned opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, anyway, your question is very difficult for this witness to answer. The question is whether these prisoners were the ultimate responsibility of Mr. Deronjic or were they the ultimate responsibility of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Based on this decision placing -- which was from the president of the RS at the time, it's obviously a binding decision, as we all know by now. And it would appear to me, at least from reading it, that this gentleman might be able to shed some light. I mean, we can't -- it can't hurt to hear his opinion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will see how far we could go, but there is some implications in your question. If Mr. Deronjic has the ultimate responsibility, do you mean that there's no responsibility at all for Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that, Your Honour. I'm not saying that at all. My question wasn't that they -- that there's no other shared responsibility, obviously there is. But -- I mean, there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's why I'm asking these sorts of questions. They're based on testimony that was brought up by the Prosecution, which I suspect they're going to be arguing at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I've already said we'll see how far we could go concerning this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, do you need the Defence counsel to repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you may answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will answer. Just as all of you agreed, I will join you in saying that it is a very complex issue, and it's hard to give a yes or no answer. However, I think - and I think a lot of people would agree with me - that this person is responsible, based on this decision. But that doesn't mean that others were not responsible as well, others who could have done something to the people who were prisoners of war at the time, whether these other people were civilians or military servicemen, it doesn't matter. But everybody is partially responsible for prisoners of war. Some people have to provide certain living conditions for them, they have to ensure their security based on various conventions, and then some people are just responsible for ensuring that no harm is done to prisoners of war. Now, whether these other people are generals or just plain guards, I don't think that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, in your capacity as the -- as a jurist, as a judge, during the -- those years on the military court and then later on as the chief military prosecutor, did you become acquainted at all with the various legal instruments and instructions that were part of or the body of law forming the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the majority of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I were to pose some questions to you with respect to the security organ, do you think you might be able to assist us on how the security organ functioned, for instance, within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could be of much assistance in that regard. At the time I worked in court, and I wasn't really acquainted with security organs at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your duty as a judge, I would suspect there were times when you had to analyse documents. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Laws and regulations?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Instructions?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I were to show you an instruction that was prepared by Mladic called the Instruction on Management and Command of Security Intelligence Agencies of the Republika Srpska, that has been admitted into evidence as D22, do you think that you might be able to look at it and give us your informed, analytical, legal opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has already responded that he is not in the position to be of much assistance on issues regarding the security organ and how they functioned within the VRS. Now Mr. Karnavas is asking him if he can analyse a legal document. You know, it's true that the witness is lawyer, but I don't know if we can -- if Mr. Karnavas should be permitted to ask him opinion on every legal issue that has arisen in this case and is likely to arise in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe you greatly expanded the scope of the cross-examination. This witness is -- was a prosecutor, a judge. You may ask some questions concerning of the criminal law or the related documents or instructions, but this question is too general and I do not know whether this witness is capable to answer this question -- or even if he answered whether there's any weight in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, for the record I wanted to show the gentleman Exhibit D22 and show him various parts. He is a jurist. I thought we might take advantage of his knowledge and expertise, since we have him here. They brought him all the way from Bosnia and Herzegovina. But if the Court wishes for me to move to another topic, I will. But my purpose was to show him one or two paragraphs, but I leave it to the Court's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. But I take it that if I were to bring an expert, I would not be denied the opportunity to pose these questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think this witness is testifying as an expert of the legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was under the impression he was a military judge, so everything comes -- everything is in that. But very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were -- you were asked to look at certain portions of the RS law and in particular I believe you were shown earlier on a segment, which is marked for identification purposes as P380, and that was the guidelines were determining criteria for criminal prosecution. Do you recall being -- that was just earlier today.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular you were asked to look at one portion, and I thought we might revisit that and maybe you can give us a more expansive answer or a follow-up to what you have already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if we could present the gentleman with that exhibit, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps if you could look at -- perhaps just to re-orient yourself, I'm going to be referring to the section at the end of paragraph 13, which I believe is the third paragraph -- I mean, page 13, the last paragraph, and then go on to paragraph -- page 14, paragraphs 1 and 2, but primarily I'm going to be focusing on paragraph 2. So that would be 14. And for the English version, it would be -- I'm primarily interested in paragraph 2 on page 8. And the RN number, or ERN number is 00814384. Page 14, paragraph 2. As you will see, the very last sentence I'm primarily interested in.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 14, paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I am told by my colleague, where it talks about the failure -- the consequences for failing to file a report. Okay?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can ask you a couple of questions about that, now that you've refreshed your memory. I wanted to just give you some guidance. Now, to your understanding, a failure to report, does that mean if, for instance, the head of the security organ of a brigade is involved in activities which might amount to persecution, that an officer's failure to file such a report, if he should learn of that activity, under the RS law would that officer also be charged with and held accountable for the same crimes of the individual who was actually committing the crimes?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these instructions say that these people will be prosecuted for some of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as I read it it says that they will be held -- it "makes them answerable for these criminal offenses." That's the very last part of the sentence in that paragraph. Does that mean that they're answerable for not filing a report, or does that mean that they themselves will be found guilty of the crimes being committed by the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this means that they will be considered responsible for not preventing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming they were in a position of preventing it?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what if they were to learn of the events after the fact?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that depends on the interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, what does the RS law say about that and where might you point us --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the law of the RS provides that they can be held responsible for concealing the fact that a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But not for actually committing the crime?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, providing that they only learned about it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to put you on the spot, because obviously you're not here to take a bar examination. But when you were meeting with the Office of the Prosecution, they came several times to see you, did they ask you to go through the laws of the RS so you and Judge Aleksic could explain the law to them?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't ask any detail explanations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We can move on to another section. Now, you were shown an order by President Karadzic to do an investigation. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you shown that order back in Bijeljina, incidentally?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We couldn't find that order. To tell you the truth, I completely forgot about that order; however, then Mr. Aleksic said that as far as he could remember, there was such an order. And then I recollected that there indeed was, however we could not find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time. I don't know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, obviously at some point the order was found. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- actually, I don't know where it was found, but obviously it exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, prior to coming to The Hague last week, the week before, the week before, the week before, did the Prosecution ever contact you to show you that order?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was shown that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever asked, sir, to perhaps make some inquiries, some investigation, to find out whether that order had actually been carried out, and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? Who asked me to carry out an investigation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether they ever asked you to see whether this order had actually ever been carried out.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So assuming that -- do you know whether it was carried out?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already said that I don't know what was the fate of that order. I don't know -- I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Had you been asked by the Prosecution to look into that matter, do you think you might have been able to at least do an investigation, make some inquiries, to find out whether that order by the president was actually carried out?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite a lengthy task. Somebody could look for it and find it, go through the archives. Because as you could see, there were several persons whom that order made responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple of last questions. What kind of witness protection programme was available at the RS, say around the period after Srebrenica, should an officer wanted to file a report after learning that someone like Mladic and Beara and Popovic, who we knew was actively engaged in killings, and some of his other security -- members of the security organ and others, what kind of witness protection programme was available to -- in the RS at that time?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there was no programme for witness protection, for the simple reason that this concept of witness protection did not exist in our law until the 1st of July, 2003, when this new law on criminal procedure was adopted. Even now it is difficult to implement that system, because we lack the resources. God knows when this will take effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Finally, you mentioned this new law that came into effect back in July, which as I understand is quite different from what it used to be, the criminal procedure. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, since the Dayton Accords, the office of the high representative has been more or less the occupying authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying it. But isn't it a fact that it is the office of the high representative that imposes law on a routine basis, including this particular law?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how I would put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.
