utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because officially that's not the case; it's not even considered a protectorate, at least not officially. And as a lawyer and somebody who works there, I am responsible for upholding the law, and I think it's more of a political issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But the -- as you well know, since the time that the office of the high representative was created for the purposes of implementing Dayton, they have been engaged, almost on a daily basis, on judicial reform. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the major aspects of the judicial reform was investigating judges and prosecutors, some of whom who are not adequately performing their functions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many, as a result of these investigations, have lost their jobs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, there have been more than one report indicating that the judiciary during that period back then in 1995, 1996, and so on, the judiciary - when I say "judiciary," I'm also including the prosecution - was rather inconsistent [Realtime transcript read in error "persistent"] in the application of the law?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that you are right in this respect, and the very fact that the high representative had to get involved in that through the judiciary reform speaks to the fact that something had to be done. Because it was quite obvious that the judiciary was not functioning properly. This is not something we can deny, even if we wanted to. Then the whole system was overhauled. The reform is still undergoing. It's not finished yet. Precisely to reduce the influence of the politicians, to have this independent judicial council, which would be free of any influence when it came to appointing and relieving of duty the judges, to keep them totally independent of politicians. And that is obviously why the high representative had to do that, and I think he was justified in doing that. It was obviously necessary, and I have to say that even though it affects me and my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas, to interrupt. Can you take a look at line 6. It says in the transcript, was rather "persistent," and I think you said "inconsistent".

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did say "inconsistent". That was -- I was trying to be delicate with the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But it's very different to say persistent or inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes, so, just to correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which brings me back to my initial question: Back in those days in 1995 and all the way up until recently when they did -- when the high representative imposed the law, creating the high judicial and prosecutorial council, but back then specifically, the office of the -- the military prosecutor wasn't totally independent and was under certain influences, whether direct or indirect, just as many of the other judges and prosecutors throughout the RS and, might I say, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the laws themselves, the emphasis was on the independence of the judges and prosecutors in their work. But you can now look at it from another standpoint, how independent you can be if you have somebody allocate funds to you, appoint you, relieve you of your duty. If somebody has the authority to do all that, but according to the law it -- they were supposed to be independent, even at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much, and give my regards to President Aleksic when you see him in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Any cross-examination, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will try to pose a few questions and to elicit answers which would assist us in this trial. Cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we begin?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were quite a few questions that pertained to the functioning of the military judicial system in the Republika Srpska in 1995 and later on until the military prosecutor system was dissolved. I think that there were some questions which created quite a confusion, and I will now try to clear that up through my questions and your answers. Do you agree with me that in 1995 and in the time when the military judicial system existed that the continental law system applied?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the law on criminal procedure that was adopted from the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia defined two types of jurisdictions: Subject matter and territorial?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is the subject matter jurisdiction of the military judicial system, of the military judiciary?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject matter jurisdiction of the military jurisdiction -- judiciary defined the jurisdiction of the basic military courts, the first instance courts, in other words, and the second instance court which was the supreme military court. The basic military courts adjudicated in all cases in the first instance, whereas the supreme military court adjudicated on the appeals. That was the second instance. Likewise, the military Supreme Court judged the decision -- passed judgements on the appeals, according to another kind of logbook in cases involving detention or the release of detainees from detention. This was also in its jurisdiction. The supreme military court also made decisions about extraordinary legal remedies, the commutation of sentences. It also conducted administrative proceedings, whereas basic military courts in terms of subject matter jurisdiction carried out all other cases, and carried out all other tasks, for instance investigations were carried out by investigative judges and they passed first instance judges. That's the basic military courts. However, if they passed a sentence of 20 years in prison, and of course after the Dayton agreement we no longer had the death penalty, but before that they could also impose the death penalty. Then there was also the third instance which was the Supreme Court of the Republika Srpska. So that would be it as far as the subject matter is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, we are not in a hurry, so please make a pause after you hear the answer. You give the interpreter a very difficult time. And please advise this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, while we speak the same language and we always have the same problem, could you please pay attention to your monitor in front of you, on the screen in front of you, the black dot will stop moving, and then you can start giving us your answer.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can speak slowly when you answer, because everything needs to be interpreted into English. Thank you. So we understand that at that time you were a judge of the supreme military court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your previous answer, you did not have the opportunity to pass any first instance judgements -- you were not the judge of the basic military court at any time?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was for a time, but that was in the period between June and January when I was a judge of the basic military court in Srpsko Sarajevo, where in addition to carrying out investigations I also passed judgements in several cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995 you dealt with appeals as a judge of the supreme military court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the law on criminal procedure, does the subject matter jurisdiction define which cases are to be -- which criminal offenses are to be dealt with by the military court and which are to be dealt with by the civilian court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: Who was tried by military courts and who was tried by civilian courts when we are talking about perpetrators of criminal offenses?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The jurisdiction of military courts, subject matter jurisdiction, covered all military personnel who committed a crime, regardless of the nature of the crime, with the exception of -- or rather, in addition to military personnel, the military judiciary had jurisdiction over civilian persons, but only for specific crimes, such as attacks on military facilities, armed insurrection, and so on. So the criminal offenses were clearly specified. Military courts also had jurisdiction to try prisoners of war who commit crimes in their capacity of prisoners of war or who have committed criminal offenses, crimes against humanity and international law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know how long we dealt with this problem of the definition of a military person, and we really wanted to define the jurisdiction of the military judiciary. But I will now try to deal with it very briefly for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. If a civilian then, a person who has not been mobilised, who does not have the status of a soldier or an officer, commits a violent criminal offence, murder, so we are talking about crimes against a person, is that person going to be tried by a military court or a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a civilian commits the criminal offenses you just specified, crimes against a person or against life and limb, they will be tried by the regular civilian court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If such a criminal offence is committed by a reserve officer - so I'm not talking about the active-duty servicemen, but a reserve soldier who has been mobilised - who will try this reserve officer for such a crime? Would it be the civilian court or the military court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person would be tried by a military court because as soon as they are -- they come to their units after the call-up, they become military personnel. Now, whether they are in active duty or whether they are in the reserve, it doesn't mean a thing. From that moment on, from the mobilisation onwards, they are considered to be military personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we have a situation that we have come across in this case. A man is on vacation, on leave. He does not have any military tasks at that time. He is at home, and he becomes a coperpetrator in a crime, he takes part in a crime, we have the name of that person and his post. Who has subject matter jurisdiction over such a person, civilian court or a military court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this issue was subject to a lot of debate, but the opinion that prevailed in the end is that if that person was engaged in the units of the VRS, regardless of the fact whether that person was on the front line or on vacation, that a military court had jurisdiction for his trial and not the civilian court, although you can go into theoretical debates. But this was the opinion that prevailed. So we could apply this to the case that you just explained to me. That was the view taken; in other words, that the military court had jurisdiction in such cases. Of course again, I say we can now launch a long theoretical debate about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I will be right in concluding that based on the case law and instructions, the term "military person" includes also persons subject to military obligation, soldiers who do not have their wartime assignment in the unit at that time, yet they have committed a crime in that period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the case, provided that such a person had a military engagement. It is not important now whether that person was on leave, either that he doesn't have a task at that time or whether he has taken annual leave, 10, 15 days, that does not play a role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Kovacevic. Let's now take another example that we had in this case. A person subject to military obligation goes to carry out his military task, and en route to his military wartime military unit he commits a criminal offence. You will agree with me, will you not, that he is again under the jurisdiction of a military court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the status of the civilian police. A civilian police officer commits a crime against a person in 1995, so a member of a police station or of the security services centre. Who has subject matter jurisdiction over such persons, to try such persons?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the regular court, civilian court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all criminal offenses committed by civilian police come under the jurisdiction of a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it would be quite dangerous for them to be tried by military courts, because then you would have a military regime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke about the other kind of jurisdiction, that's the territorial jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to speed things up a bit, I will just gloss over this issue of territorial jurisdiction; you correct me if I'm wrong. Military judiciary was organised on the basis of corps, as regards the territorial jurisdiction. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The court that had jurisdiction for the 1st and 2nd corps was the military court in Banja Luka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The court that had territorial jurisdiction for the Eastern Bosnia Corps was the military court in Bijeljina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The court that had jurisdiction after the Drina Corps and for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps until its dissolution was the military court in Srpsko Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The court that had jurisdiction over the Herzegovina Corps was - during the war - the military court in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as we understand, in 1995, let's say in mid-1995, the military court in Srpsko Sarajevo ceased to exist. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that from that time onwards, the territorial jurisdiction for the Drina Corps, for all practical purposes, became divided?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the division was based on the territorial principle that followed the organisation of the civilian district courts?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. Now, I can't tell you whether it was like that 100 per cent, but that would be the territorial jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us be more specific. After the dissolution of the military court in Srpsko Sarajevo, according to the territorial jurisdiction, the territory of municipalities, the sociopolitical organisations, that's what we're talking about, Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik came under the territorial jurisdiction of the military court in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the municipalities of Vlasenica, Sekovici, Han Pijesak, Skelani, for as long as they existed as a territorial organisation, Visegrad, Rogatica, Sokolac, that all belonged to the Drina Corps were now under the military court in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now just to simplify things, to have a specific example, who has jurisdiction to try a case involving a person subject to military obligation belonging to a unit in Visegrad or in Vlasenica, the brigades there, commits a criminal offence in the territory of Srebrenica, Bratunac, or Zvornik. Let's go back now to the issue of subject matter jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we have to see the site where the crime was committed. The jurisdiction would fall to Bijeljina. So the jurisdiction was always determined by the location where the crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I -- we just have to now make the division between the pre-trial -- pre-criminal proceedings and criminal proceedings, per se. Who actually detected war crimes -- who actually detected crimes in the system of military judiciary? Who was tasked with that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the basic organs in this system, and that would be the military police. And at that time, part of the security also dealt with that. As far as I know, it was also in their jurisdiction; in other words, detecting crimes. That would be the basic thing, the basic organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right to conclude that the military prosecutor's office, in order to detect the perpetrators of a crime and to gather evidence and material facts that would -- that could enable the military prosecutor to file an indictment, would be in something that the military police and the security organs would carry out. They are the organs that the prosecutor will task with finding the appropriate information, which would enable the military prosecutor to initiate proceedings and ultimately perhaps to file an indictment?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would be requested to do so through the commands of appropriate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely, yes. Everything went through the commands of these units?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I then turn this issue around? If a unit wanted to file a criminal report against their member -- against its member because they had -- such a member committed a criminal offence, would this criminal report be filed through the command of the unit?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the conclusion would be correct that if a member of the Zvornik Brigade wanted to file a criminal report against his commanding officer for reasonable suspicion that a crime has been committed, a war crime or a crime against property, the official criminal report should be filed through the brigade command, where it would receive the appropriate official seal, among other things?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the regular route. But like in the civilian system, you can file a criminal report which does not bear the official seal. But this, what you say, is the regular route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the regular procedure is such that the criminal report has to go through the brigade command and has to bear the signature of the brigade commander and the appropriate seal?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But if the military prosecutor receives a criminal report that has come through any route whatsoever, he is obliged to act upon it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the system of operation of the military prosecutor's office, has it ever happened that the military prosecutor applied to the civilian organs, civilian prosecution organs, in order to obtain information that were relevant for the commission of a crime?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in cases where the military police and the military security was unable to do so, or did it happen for some other reason that we had these parallel structures. Or to -- let me rephrase that. Why would the military prosecutor ask a civilian police to gather information instead of asking it from the military police, which is the way that the usual procedure was?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the cases where the prosecutor decided that civilian police had such information and that it was easier for civilian police to gather such material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, it's time for the break. And we'll resume at 12.30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for people's schedule, we don't have another witness this afternoon. We're hoping to get that witness tomorrow, but the weather is very bad in the UK, and we'll keep you abreast of those plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, let us resume where we ended before the break. So we spoke about the fact that upon receiving a criminal complaint, military prosecutor will request military police and military security organs to collect facts on the crime committed, the perpetrator, and any other evidence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us try and illustrate it through a particular situation. Officially or unofficially, as you have stated, a member of the Zvornik Brigade files a criminal complaint with the relevant military prosecutor, which in this case would be the one in Bijeljina, for a war crime committed by somebody -- in fact, committed by members of the military police and security organs of the Zvornik Brigade. What can the military prosecutor do under such circumstances? Who will he ask to gather information on perpetrators? It's an absurd situation.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation is complex, but it all depends on the prosecutor. It depends on his skills and abilities to find a way to prove that this had been committed. It would be similar to saying that in peacetime we cannot prosecute officers of civilian police, and as you know, we do have such cases. And, of course, these cases are complex, they are not typical cases, but they do exist. It doesn't mean that this cannot be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for example, a criminal report is filed by a member of the Zvornik Brigade against security organs of the Drina Corps and an officer of the Main Staff of that corps, charging them with a war crime. What would a military prosecutor be able to do under such circumstances? And I'm here referring to the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I've already answered that question, too. There are various possibilities here. Obviously he would make requests. He doesn't have to address that particular security organ -- that particular military police, because information can be gathered in other ways. It is a more complex situation, but it all depends on the prosecutor, how he will use his skills to resolve the situation. I think it would be absurd to say, Oh my God, if a crime is committed by a member of security, we will forego all other work. We won't file any criminal reports and so on. I don't think that this would be the right approach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Naturally this is not why I was putting this question to you; this was not a trick question. I simply wanted to hear your answer. I wanted you to confirm that it would be very difficult for military prosecutor under those circumstances to identify the perpetrator and gather evidence and facts. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entirely agree with you. The job of the military prosecutor would be made much more difficult under those circumstances. There would be various dangers, various risks, especially in wartime. This makes the situation much more complex than under normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what we precisely wanted to say is that a person filing a criminal report against a member of security organs or military police for being coperpetrators or perpetrators of a crime, in view of what you told us, that there was no witness protection system, there was no protection envisioned for a person filing a criminal report under those circumstances, that would all mean that a person filing a criminal report would be exposed to significant danger. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he probably wouldn't be having a great time. And as to the level of danger, I couldn't say anything about that. Even in peacetime, it is not a holiday to handle a case like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said this, that for example if the person filing a criminal report, an officer in that unit used unorthodox ways of filing the report, for example, if he directly contacted the authorities, then it would still be difficult, and especially if he used the official routes, you know, if everything was done in a regular with seals and signatures, with records being taken and so on. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of what happened in our trial here, I would now like to draw some parallels with our case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can I please ask the assistance of the usher. I need Exhibit 5702 [as interpreted]. This is the report on criminal activities in July of 1995. Could we please show this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you have seen this document just a while ago. Could we please comment on it. Third page, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I think the number is wrong, Mr. Stojanovic. It should be 702, P702, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so. That's what I said, Your Honour, 702. Perhaps it was an interpretation error. So P702.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, could we please pay attention to page 3 in B/C/S version. The last three digits are 326. Please take a look at paragraph 6. It says: "Homicide, crimes against persons." It says there: "VTK463/95," and a request was filed to launch an investigation against Stevanovic, Stanko, son of Tomislav. Born in 1968 in the municipality of Travnik, due to probable cause that he has committed on the 23rd of July, 1997, at around 2400 hours in a bar." I don't want to read everything. He, using a fire weapon, wounded Kremenovic, Radoslav, and then fired three bullets into Erdemovic, Drazen, whereby he admitted a crime of attempted murder, aimed against several persons. This is under Article 2, subsection 6, of criminal code. Do you remember anything pertaining to this case?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever encounter such a case against Stevanovic, Stanko, at the second instance level for a crime committed against Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: In almost all second instance chambers -- I was a member of a chamber. There were many cases that we dealt with. This probably was not a case that I worked on. Now, whether any of my colleagues who were in other chambers encountered this case, I couldn't say. But the name of Drazen Erdemovic does ring a bell. I don't know if it was because he was an used here in The Hague or because I had something to do with this case. I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's try and clarify something. It says here that there is reasonable grounds to believe that on the 23rd of July, 1997, he committed such-and-such crime. And the report here is for July of 1995. So what do you think? Could we conclude that this was a typo, that instead of 1997 it should read 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this must be an error. I don't know whether it should read "1995" or some other year, but obviously it cannot be 1996 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, Drazen Erdemovic testified here, the one who is mentioned in this document, and during his testimony he said that this event or this crime described here as involving Stevanovic, Stanko, is directly linked to his participation in Srebrenica events and that he was implicated in this because he disagreed with the assignments given to him within his unit. This could be a hypothesis. Of course, you said you didn't know anything about the particulars of the case. Now, in view of what he said and in view of what is stated in that criminal report, does that seem plausible to you that this action would be taken against anyone who would try to raise an alarm because of something that had happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I'm afraid this last part of the question seems to call for speculation a little too much from this witness. He's already stated he doesn't know anything about the case and now the hypothetical is being drawn out even further with reports from counsel of what was said by another witness et cetera. But this witness doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. Please move on, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I fully understand the position taken by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, let me finalise this. We will use another exhibit, P712. So P712, this is the document containing the order of the president of the republic on investigating the events in Pilica. And also it involves the letter sent by Predrag Drinic to the Main Staff of the VRS. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that you hadn't seen this document sent by Predrag Drinic to the Main Staff before. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you saw it just now, just recently?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us please see how the pre-trial proceedings and the trial itself look like in practice. According to the president of the republic, a commission was to be established in order to look into events and facts surrounding the two corpses that were found in Pilica, in Zvornik municipality. As the commission was not established on the 26th of March, 1996, the military prosecutor requested the Main Staff of the VRS to establish a part of the commission through the security and information department. And these people would conduct investigation on the ground and gather information and facts concerning this event. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the information that we have available to us, the 10th Sabotage Detachment participated in these events in Pilica. This 10th Sabotage Detachment was under the security and intelligence department. Does it seem bizarre to you that this security and intelligence department is requested to establish a commission which would investigate the crime in which these same people might have participated?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I've already answered that. It is obvious that this is a very complex route, but it is also obvious that the prosecutor is trying, to the best of his abilities, to resolve and determine what had happened. He believed that this was the best possible route, because the previous commission had done nothing. Now, whether this turned out to be effective or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that based on the logbook of criminal activity, there obviously was no effect, because as you told us yourself, there were no criminal reports filed nor criminal investigation carried out and there were no indictments issued. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in this case they failed to even determine where these corpses had come from. There were two corpses involved. And yes, that's true, there were no criminal reports filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct, Ms. Davis?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I do have a brief re-direct. Re-examined by Ms. Davis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, a few moments ago before the last break, you were asked by Mr. Stojanovic about which court, the civilian court or the military court, would have certain jurisdiction over certain individuals. And you were asked one point about the civilian police officer who may have committed murder or a violent crime and who would have jurisdiction over that individual. I believe your answer was that civilian courts would have jurisdiction. My question to you is: If a civilian police officer had been working with the military in a criminal operation, who would have had jurisdiction over that civilian police officer?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the jurisdiction is concerned, there are some provisions that say that if a crime is committed simultaneously, both by a military person and a civilian person, so the same crime but committed together by them, in that case, the military court would have jurisdiction. However, this is an exception. Because the policeman at the time the crime is committed is a civilian, even though he's wearing a uniform. However, if the crime is committed in the company of a military serviceman, then the military court would have jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Does it follow then that a civilian police officer who's working under the command of a military unit with other military officers or soldiers in a criminal operation would also fall under the jurisdiction of a military court?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Providing they committed the crime together. However, if the policeman commits a crime on his own, alone, then the civilian regular court would be in charge of it. So they have to be also linked by the crime as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The last thing that I wanted to address with you is just to clarify something that I think has become unnecessarily confusing. In order to do that, I'd like for you to be shown again Exhibit P702. And if you can look at the first page of the report -- of the actual report, not the cover page, the last paragraph on the page is the one that I directed you towards during my direct examination. We discussed this earlier, that there was a mention in this report of the fact that the jurisdiction of the military court in Bijeljina had been expanded and now incorporated some region covered by the Drina Corps. Is that right? Have I summarised that correctly from before?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you indicated to us that when that division of the Drina Corps region had happened, that some of those -- some of the Drina Corps geographic area, for lack of a better term, had gone to the Bijeljina court and some to another court. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the areas of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik you have clarified for us a number of times now, came under the Bijeljina jurisdiction, after that expansion of the military court jurisdiction in Bijeljina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this report of course was produced in July 1995. So I take it we can assume from this that the expansion of the area of jurisdiction of the military court in Bijeljina happened prior to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the reason I wanted to clarify this with you is I wanted to ask you if you remembered when we were meeting the other day that you were shown some monthly reports, not only from the Bijeljina district but also from the Sarajevo district. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall that the monthly reports that you were shown were for the months July 1995 through December 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you reviewed those reports, and you didn't find any investigations into war crimes -- reports or investigations or prosecutions into war crimes in those monthly reports either. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So based on those monthly reports, it seems that the Srpsko Sarajevo military court district was still in existence through 1995, but would you agree with me that the expansion of the jurisdiction of the military court in Bijeljina happened before July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already discussed this. I cannot remember the exact date, but if you allow me. I don't think that is of vital importance here. What's important is that subject matter jurisdiction was given to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from Judges? It seems to me there's no questions. Well, at this stage are there any documents to tender, Ms. Davis?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: We do have a number of documents, Your Honour. P380 has already been admitted into evidence. So we'll begin with P702, P703, P704, P706, P707, P708, P710, P711, P712 under seal, P713, P714, and P715.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour. But perhaps I could remind that one of these exhibits has been admitted yesterday as the Defence exhibit. It was given a D67/3 identification number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So those documents tendered by the Prosecution are admitted into evidence. Are there documents to tender by the Defence counsel through this witness? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, just if Mr. Blagojevic is going to go into more personal information about Defence counsel, I would prefer not be present for the Prosecution to hear that. I just -- it's getting a little inappropriate at this point. I don't know what he's going to say, but I'm not really sure we should be here when he goes into those sorts of areas. I know it's impossible to predict, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Blagojevic, would you please tell me what is the main subject of your intervention. What are you going to talk about? THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's going to be quite simple. I simply wanted to ask, and I'm going to ask the Prosecution, to be quite specific about the actual article and paragraph in the law indicating that the military courts have jurisdiction over police officers in the specific case presented by the witness and when such a situation occurred in practice for a civilian police officer, a member of the civilian police. So I want the exact law of the Republika Srpska with the exact article and paragraph in order to corroborate this, in order not to have the situation in which this situation would act as the legislator, the ultimate legislator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, I think this issue has been brought up and discussed during the direct and cross-examination with this witness. This witness has answered this question so far as to his own knowledge. The Prosecution actually is not a witness in this case. And after this sitting, we'll go over the transcript to see how this witness answered that question. Of course your question has already been registered in the transcript. At the same time, I would like to remind you - as I did before many times - if you have some questions or if you have some problems with the Prosecution or with the witness, please put it down on a piece of paper and the guard will send it to your counsel, as Mr. Jokic did in this case. Well, thank you, Witness, for coming to The Hague to give your testimony. We hope you have a pleasant journey back home. The usher will show you out of the room. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since we have a little time left for this morning's sitting, there's several procedural matters that I would like to deal with, making the best use of the time left. The first question I would like to address to the Prosecution about the two remaining witnesses we discussed the other day. Could you please give us a kind of indication how soon or when are you expecting them to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is still a little unclear, though it is our intention to have them here no later in a month, hopefully in about three weeks. Three, three and a half weeks is what the time frame that we think would be reasonable enough to be able to give the government a chance to get passports, find them, serve them, and get arrangements made. If it can be any sooner, we'll try that as well. And -- but we certainly don't want it to go beyond a month. If it can be done, it should be able to be done in a month, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask Defence counsel for Mr. Blagojevic that from yesterday or the other day's statement you made in this courtroom, could we understand that you will allow the Bench to hear this witness while you are preparing or submitting your 98 bis motions. If there is some new evidence appearing in their testimony, the Bench will give you permission to file some attachments or addendum to your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was hoping that you would not have interpreted my explanation in that fashion, but I can see where the Court is going. What I was hoping is that we would be working on that 98 bis motion. We do -- we take it very, very seriously. We have a very large volume of material to go through. And in light of the Prosecution's dilemma, given that we are being somewhat magnanimous at this point, I thought that we would enjoy a certain degree of flexibility on the part of -- from the Trial Chamber in perhaps allowing us some additional time to really get in -- a very serious motion in. We think that the two weeks that's allotted is slightly -- it's tight. It's very tight. With this new information, we don't know. So we -- obviously we hope to have it in or about the time the Prosecution will have its witnesses. I mean, we can have it earlier if the Court orders us to do so, but we were kind of hoping for that sort of flexibility, so to speak. And I certainly don't want to file a motion prior to hearing these witnesses, because then it allows the Prosecutor -- I don't want to say it unfair, but perhaps an advantage that they normally would not enjoy. And I'm sure that Mr. McCloskey would not try to take advantage of the situation, but nonetheless I think that as a good Prosecutor if he's going to avail himself to the information that I put before him. So that's why I would wish to have the opportunity to have that information -- to have the witnesses first testify and then us filing the motion. Because the only other alternative would be for us to file it under seal, wait until that testimony, and then have it released to the Prosecutor, so they don't have any unfair advantage as a result of having our motion prior to putting on these witnesses. Because it may generate a certain line of questioning that they normally would not have or another request for additional witnesses. So in any event, I think if the Prosecution has made already efforts to get those folks over here, which I am sure they have, I see no reason why they can't be here in an additional week's time from what you had anticipated us having for filing that motion. So in a round about way what I'm saying, Mr. President, I'm trying to take advantage of the situation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand your position. Mr. Stojanovic, what's your view on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite frankly, I believe that the two witnesses have no specific relevance to -- for the indictment against Dragan Jokic. I know that what one of the witnesses will be saying, as explained by the Prosecution. And as for the testimony of the other witness who is, if I understand it correctly, belongs to the Bratunac Brigade, I don't know about that. But I am willing to believe that they do not have anything to do with Dragan Jokic. We are now between co-counsels from Mrs. Sinatra to Mr. Lukic, and we have been working on this since yesterday, scanning all the documents. And we are working on our 98 bis motion. We believe that we will be able to file it by the 20th of February -- 28th of February. We know the importance of this filing. And if the Prosecution would be able to bring the witnesses, the two witnesses, within the next two or maybe three weeks, as the Prosecutor said, that would mean that the witnesses would be here sometime in mid-February. Because the Prosecution will be presenting its case throughout the next week, and I would like to propose the Prosecution and Mr. Karnavas for professional reasons, I would like to -- the deadline for us to start from that time, the 15-day deadline. Because then, instead of the deadline being the 20th, we would have the deadline of the end of the month for that filing. We believe that it really would be fair and that would also play into the hand of the Prosecution, because the Prosecution would then be able to extend its time period in which it can present its case, which is what they applied for. But at any rate, Mr. Jokic's Defence, in light of the fact that the testimonies will not have any bearing on Mr. Jokic, will be ready to present this motion as requested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Well, I understand that the position of the -- of Mr. Karnavas, because your 98 bis motion should be filed only after we hear all the Prosecution's witnesses. And I hope if we could hear those two witnesses sometime in the middle or later February, the Defence counsel should file their 98 bis motion the next day after we hear those two witnesses. Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was thinking more like three or -- three to five days after. I mean, the next day, where I hear them, I have to process the information, I may need to rework the motion a little bit. So it's not a matter of -- because one of the witnesses, and I assume that the Prosecution's motion for this additional time is a serious one because one of them happens to be the driver for Mr. Blagojevic, otherwise they would -- they certainly would take him off the list. So I can only suspect that the Prosecution thinks that these witnesses are relevant to their case in-chief. So I think a three-day deadline, although cutting it close, I would prefer five, to be honest with you. But I will settle for three. But one is cutting it too close, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe the main body of your motion has already been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I thank you, Mr. President, for the confidence that you have in me. But I think three days would be a reasonable amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've come down from five to three, I'm meeting you half way. From one -- between one and five is three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you know I'm not good at bargaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But three days seems to me is reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So the three-day extension is extended. But at the same time, I would like to remind the parties that the practiced direction on the length of the briefs and motions provides that the motions should not exceed ten pages. In the previous case, there are very lengthy motions on that, some of them even more than 100 pages, which is a great burden to the Chamber. Of course we understand that this case is a very complicated case involving a lot of evidence in it. So if the Defence teams would like to ask for an extension of the pages, I hope you could consider it and inform us orally sometime next week. But you have to remember that the request of extension of the pages should be reasonable. Well, since we are approaching to the end of the Prosecution's case, I believe that the preparations of the Defence case also should be taken into consideration. According to our previous decision, the preliminary list of witnesses for the Defence case should be submitted on the 8th of March, 2004, a pre-Defence conference scheduled on the 17th of March, 2004. And the start of Mr. Blagojevic's case will be on the 19th March, 2004. As for the list of the witnesses, I would like to remind the Defence team to the Rule 65 ter (G)(i) on these particular issues. I hope the Defence could give us some sort of summary of the facts on which its witnesses will testify. Also specify the category of the witnesses, for instance, the expert, military, human personnel. And also indicate the points of the indictments as to which each witness will testify. Of course we would like to know the final total numbers of the witnesses. If there are any witnesses that the Defence counsel would like to introduce through 92 bis or videolink witnesses, we would like to be informed earlier so that the necessary preparations could be underway. We also hope the Defence counsel could estimate the length of the time required for each witness as well as the total time estimated for the presentation of the Defence case. If there is a request for subpoenas, a motion should be filed a month in advance. And time should be given as well in respect of requests for safe conduct, if there is any. Regarding the 92 bis motion, a 14-day notice must be given to the opposing party, and that time is further needed once it is granted for the Registrar to assign a presiding officer. And I hope that the parties could meet in order to determine for which document the Prosecution may raise objections to its authenticity. And we also would like to ask the Defence team sometime later to indicate to the Bench whether their clients would like to make a statement under Rule 94 bis. Well, these are all the matters I would like to say at this stage. Are there any other issues that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, on that subject that you were mentioning, as I think we all know, under 67(B) the reciprocal -- excuse me 67(C), the reciprocal discovery section. And both sides have invoked reciprocal discovery, and under the rule it says that the Prosecution should be allowed to review and inspect any materials the Defence expects to use as evidence. We have not made any time frame at this point and have not tried to suggest a time frame. But I think as we're coming to their case, an appropriate time frame for that should be made. And so I would suggest as soon as possible so that we can be properly prepared for cross-examination of the Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think after the 6th of February the parties should meet to discuss this matter. And I'll instruct the Senior Legal Officer to hold a 65 ter meeting with the parties. During that meeting, if you or the parties have any issues to raise, you may raise it first there. Of course the Bench will be ready to assist the two parties, especially the Defence team to present their case; although the Defence has no obligation to present the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just ask one question, Your Honour. On that point, if the Defence is planning to put on an alibi Defence, they do have an obligation - as I know the Court is aware - and I believe it's long past the deadline for that. So can I now assume that there will not be an alibi defence an either part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that's too early. I think the -- especially in the Jokic case, I think their case will still be at least two months later than that. Is that my understanding that Mr. Karnavas will present his case first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I will be presenting it, though I probably would venture to say that it's going to be slightly longer than the two months that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Rule regarding alibis, Rule 67, and it begins with 67(A) and says as early as reasonably practicable in any event prior to the commencement of the trial." And then point ii, "The Defence shall notify the Prosecutor of its intent to offer: (a) the defence of alibi." So all I was saying that is since we're well into the trial and the Defence has not offered any defence of alibi, I think it would be fair for the Prosecutor to know, and in fact, and in law, that there will be no alibi defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as early as possible does not set a specific date on that. In my previous case, in some situations it's one month before they are presenting their case. Do you think one month will be enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it says "before the trial". We have already been in and are relying on the fact that there would be no alibi defence. I have had bad luck with this in my former life where there is a similar requirement, and I would just -- we have been relying on the firmness of this Rule. If that is being changed by the Court, we would certainly like to know about it, because it is a rather significant issue. And I see Mr. Blagojevic has raised his hand as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me first hear Mr. Karnavas on this issue -- no, Mr. Blagojevic, please wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, with respect to alibi, and I can understand the Prosecutor's concern, normally that issue where it comes from the jurisdiction that he practices, the main concern is to allow the Prosecutor enough time to investigate the alibi witness or witnesses. So that's the whole purpose of that particular Rule. In this case the Prosecution is still putting on its case. They just indicated that they're going to be introducing some witnesses, one of whom was the driver for Mr. Blagojevic, who at least with respect to one particular day or part of a day, will testify to, I assume, the whereabouts of Mr. Blagojevic. I think by this point in time, the Prosecution is well aware of the theory of our particular defence and of what we have been maintaining the entire time. So that's as far as I am prepared to go at this point in time. Now, when we do have our witness list, we will give it to the Prosecutor, we will give a summary as to what they will be saying, they will have sufficient time to investigate the backgrounds and to meet with these people if they so desire. But I think at this point in time, that is as prepared as I am to answer this question, particularly given that Mr. McCloskey has not given me any forewarning that he wanted to have a discussion on this particular issue. But I can assure Mr. McCloskey that the Defence, at least with respect to Mr. Blagojevic, does not intend to engage in any, you know guerilla warfare as far as, you know, in trying to sabotage them or trying to, you know, hide the evidence from them. That's not my practice, it has never been, it won't be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I hear you on this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the view of the Defence regarding each of the counts of the indictment are quite clear. They have been expressed in our pre-trial brief. We specified quite clearly why we deem Mr. Dragan Jokic to be not guilty on any count of the indictment. We state that Dragan Jokic did not exist [as interpreted] and that he was not in the area. We think it is now too early for us to take a stand, in light of the Rule 67, and I think that at the time when we start presenting our case, which will be in less than -- it won't be taking place even in four months, we will have quite enough time from the 8th of March [as interpreted], when we will be giving the list of witnesses with the summaries of their statements and indicating what -- why we're calling the witnesses to prove what. I believe that the Prosecution will be informed at all times of our intentions. In the three years that all of us have been involved in this case, the Prosecution and the Defence, I think that we are quite familiar with the case of the Prosecution, and the Prosecution is well aware of the case that the Defence is going to present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is getting to be a very serious matter. That sounded to me like an alibi defence. This is the first time I've anything that sounded like an alibi defence. He said his person wasn't there at the time. Now, the law is as clear as clear can be, that once -- that they have a duty to tell us about alibi defences prior to the trial. I did not bring a motion because I believe that they were honourable men, and now I'm hearing right before our case that he is going to give an alibi. It's not just that. Once they do tell us they have an alibi they shall: "Specify the place or places at which the accused claims to be present at the time of the alleged crimes and the names and addresses of witnesses and other evidence upon which the accused intends to rely to establish the alibi --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Having failed to present us with this defence at this time, there is very strong grounds to not allow them to put on that defence at all, which I'm not going to push that, that's not my style. But I would like, and I would -- we can file a motion if you feel necessary, I would like and would request that the Court order them to provide -- to obey the law that is laid down as clear as a bell and tell us if they have an alibi or not. And then if they do, as it seems that Mr. Stojanovic does, then meet the details of that as soon as possible. Mr. Karnavas has not said whether he has an alibi or not. If he wants to stand up and say that his client was in and around the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the 11th or 12th, 13th, then we don't have a problem. But if he's got an alibi, we need to hear about it, and the law says we have that right to hear about it. And this is not some new law. This is a very serious matter and I would hope we can get a very clear ruling on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe there is very limited time for us to go around the debate concerning the issue of the reciprocal disclosure as well as the meaning of the alibi at this stage. So I hope that we could find another time, maybe through a 65 ter meeting, to discuss this matter between the parties first, otherwise we'll stay here for the whole day on this issue. Mr. Stojanovic, if you insist, I give you one minute, very concise, because we will have another opportunity to bring up this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will make maximum use of it. I never, ever -- did not say what the Prosecution just said. I do not mean to use any illicit means in my defence. The issue of alibi is -- remains open. We have a different definition of alibi. If my client is charged with conducting the operation in Orahovac on the 14th and if another document indicates that he was in the Zvornik Brigade command, then it is quite clear what I'm trying to prove. Because a man cannot physically be present at two places. So the issue of alibi has already been breached -- or broached, I'm sorry. Our defence is quite clear. We have given a written -- handwritten document a few days ago. What we want to establish right from the beginning is the exact position of Dragan Jokic. We don't want to go into that now, but I want to assure the Prosecutor that I will never use any illicit, illicit means and I assure you that I intend to go on in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Blagojevic. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just want to give my clear view on the future of this trial. I have nobody to prepare my case with, the defence case, and I want to state that quite clearly. If this situation continues, I will enter that stage unprepared. I don't want to do that because my situation is quite complex as it is. I would like to have as few problems as possible. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you've raised this issue many times before. I don't think it's necessary for you to raise it whenever you have a chance to take the floor. And this Bench has already explained to you the decisions by the Appeals Chamber. I will not spend one more word on this very issue. Well, if there is nothing else -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted to give you an update on our situation with witnesses. We have one more witness. Last heard she's sitting on an airplane unable to take off but if -- from the UK because of weather. But we hope she will get here today and we'll put her on tomorrow. And if I hear of any further problems, I will let the Court and counsel know as soon as I hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a couple of brief matters. First of all, I'm told by Ms. Tomanovic that apparently when the translation -- in the translation March was translated into May, but the deadlines were March -- I mean, May as opposed to March. So just to make sure that Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic know that it's March and not May. I think it was March 8th and it was translated into May 8th. Secondly, I had brought up the issue of a previous witness that was -- the Prosecution suggested be brought into court under 92 bis. I did alert the Prosecution. I did alert someone from Chambers in court a few days ago. And I just want to go on the record. This is with respect to Ms. Ibrahimafendic. And I was given a week or so to file a motion. That deadline was on Monday. Prior to Monday, I had an opportunity to go back and re-read a couple of times the testimony given by that witness, taking into consideration Your Honour's comments from the Bench. And in light of re-reading the testimony in the previous case and in light of Your Honour's remarks and in keeping in mind the Prosecutor's remarks as well, I came to the conclusion that this witness -- that I need not file a motion and that I would withdraw my initial -- my earlier request. And therefore, I concur with the Court's opinion that this witness can come in through 92 bis, as suggested by the Prosecution. So I just wanted to go on record with that and also alert the Court that it wasn't a lapse of diligence for not filing that motion in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. And we'll resume tomorrow morning, if possible, at 9.00 in Courtroom II. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 1.43 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of January, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
